```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Estimate one buffalo's home range with MCP, KDE (two bandwidths),
a Brownian bridge and AKDE; map them together and explain why they differ;
use variograms to tell a resident from a nomad; and test every estimator
against a simulated animal whose true home range we know.

**Time:** ~70 minutes. **Packages:** `adehabitatHR`, `adehabitatLT`, `ctmm`,
`amt`, `sf`, `dplyr`, `ggplot2`.
:::

```{r}
library(adehabitatHR)
library(adehabitatLT)
library(ctmm)
library(amt)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Setup — one buffalo

```{r}
buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier, t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(id, t)

cilla <- buffalo |> filter(id == "Cilla")

# Projected coordinates (UTM 36S) for adehabitatHR, which assumes a plane
cilla_utm <- st_as_sf(cilla, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(32736)
xy <- st_coordinates(cilla_utm)
pts <- SpatialPoints(xy, proj4string = CRS("EPSG:32736"))

nrow(cilla)
range(cilla$t)
```

::: {.callout-note}
`adehabitatHR` predates `sf` and expects `sp` objects — hence
`SpatialPoints()`. This is the "messy history" from Session 2 in practice.
:::

## Task 1 — Five estimates of one home range

### MCP and KDE

```{r}
mcp95 <- mcp(pts, percent = 95)
area_mcp <- mcp.area(pts, percent = 95, unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]]

kd_href <- kernelUD(pts, h = "href", grid = 300, extent = 1)
kd_lscv <- kernelUD(pts, h = "LSCV", grid = 300, extent = 1)

area_href <- kernel.area(kd_href, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
area_lscv <- kernel.area(kd_lscv, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]

c(h_ref_m = kd_href@h$h, h_lscv_m = kd_lscv@h$h,
  lscv_converged = kd_lscv@h$convergence)
```

### Brownian bridge

The bridge needs the *trajectory*, not just the points, and two variance
parameters: `sig2`, the location error (we assume ~30 m for GPS), and `sig1`,
the animal's mobility, which `liker()` estimates by maximum likelihood.

```{r}
#| cache: true
ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(xy), date = cilla$t, id = "Cilla")
lik <- liker(ltr, sig2 = 30, rangesig1 = c(1, 100), plotit = FALSE)
lik$Cilla$sig1

bb <- kernelbb(ltr, sig1 = lik$Cilla$sig1, sig2 = 30, grid = 300, extent = 0.3)
area_bb <- kernel.area(bb, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
```

### AKDE

`ctmm` fits a continuous-time movement model first. It wants Movebank-style
columns and works in geographic coordinates.

```{r}
#| cache: true
tel <- as.telemetry(
  data.frame(timestamp = cilla$t, location.long = cilla$x, location.lat = cilla$y,
             individual.local.identifier = "Cilla"),
  timeformat = "auto")

guess <- ctmm.guess(tel, interactive = FALSE)   # not variogram.fit(): that opens a GUI
fit   <- ctmm.select(tel, guess)
ak    <- akde(tel, fit)

summary(fit)
akde_ci <- summary(ak, units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6   # m² -> km²
akde_ci
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not use `variogram.fit()` in a script

It opens an interactive slider window for choosing starting values by eye —
great at the console, fatal in a rendered document. `ctmm.guess(...,
interactive = FALSE)` gives the same starting values automatically.
:::

### Your turn

**1a.** Put all five 95% areas in one table. **1b.** Did LSCV converge?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
areas <- data.frame(
  estimator = c("MCP 95%", "KDE h_ref", "KDE LSCV", "Brownian bridge", "AKDE"),
  area_km2  = round(c(area_mcp, area_href, area_lscv, area_bb, akde_ci[2])),
  low_km2   = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, round(akde_ci[1])),
  high_km2  = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, round(akde_ci[3]))
)
areas
```

A factor of about four between the smallest and largest estimate, for the same
animal and the same fixes. LSCV **did not converge** — `kernelUD()` warned —
and chose a bandwidth of about 100 m, which splits the range into fragments
around clusters of consecutive fixes. Only AKDE comes with a confidence
interval.
:::

**1c.** Show yourself the autocorrelation problem: thin the fixes and watch
the KDE area.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
thin_tab <- lapply(c(1, 2, 6, 12, 24, 48), function(k) {
  keep <- seq(1, nrow(xy), by = k)
  a <- kernel.area(kernelUD(SpatialPoints(xy[keep, ]), h = "href", grid = 200),
                   percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
  data.frame(every_nth_fix = k, fixes = length(keep), kde95_km2 = round(a))
}) |> bind_rows()
thin_tab
```

If the fixes were independent draws from a fixed UD, the estimate would
stabilise as you add data. Instead the densest data give the **smallest**
range: every extra autocorrelated fix adds almost no new information but makes
the estimator more confident. That is exactly the bias AKDE corrects.
:::

## Task 2 — Map them together

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: center
contour_sf <- function(ud, label) {
  st_as_sf(getverticeshr(ud, percent = 95)) |>
    st_set_crs(32736) |> mutate(estimator = label) |> select(estimator)
}

contours <- bind_rows(
  st_as_sf(mcp95) |> st_set_crs(32736) |> mutate(estimator = "MCP 95%") |> select(estimator),
  contour_sf(kd_href, "KDE h_ref"),
  contour_sf(kd_lscv, "KDE LSCV"),
  contour_sf(bb, "Brownian bridge"),
  as.sf(ak, level.UD = 0.95) |> st_transform(32736) |>
    filter(grepl("est", name)) |> mutate(estimator = "AKDE") |> select(estimator)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = cilla_utm, size = 0.1, alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_sf(data = contours, aes(colour = estimator), fill = NA, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("MCP 95%" = "grey20", "KDE h_ref" = "#1f6f78",
                                 "KDE LSCV" = "#6fc3cd", "Brownian bridge" = "#b8860b",
                                 "AKDE" = "#c1440e")) +
  coord_sf(crs = 32736) +
  labs(title = "Cilla: five 95% home ranges", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## To hand in

This map, and **one paragraph** explaining why the five estimates differ. For
each estimator name the question it answers and the assumption it makes about
the fixes. This comparison — not any single number — is the point of the
session.
:::

## Task 3 — Variograms: is there a home range at all?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
data(gazelle)
gz <- gazelle[[1]]

vg_cilla <- variogram(tel)
vg_gz    <- variogram(gz)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(vg_cilla, CTMM = fit, fraction = 0.5, main = "Buffalo 'Cilla'")
plot(vg_gz, fraction = 0.5, main = "Mongolian gazelle")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### Your turn

**3a.** Which variogram levels off? **3b.** Fit a model to the gazelle and
compare its range-crossing time with the tracking duration.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Cilla's variogram rises and then **flattens**: beyond a lag of a few days her
positions are as far apart as they ever get. That asymptote *is* range
residency, and the fitted model's curve follows it.

The gazelle's variogram keeps climbing across much of the plot, with no clear
plateau.

```{r}
#| cache: true
fit_gz <- ctmm.select(gz, ctmm.guess(gz, interactive = FALSE))
summary(fit_gz)$CI[c(1, 2), ]

c(tracking_days = as.numeric(diff(range(gz$t))) / 86400)
```

The gazelle's estimated range-crossing time is months long, with a confidence
interval whose upper end exceeds the whole study. In the time it was tracked,
it crossed its "range" only a handful of times — perhaps not at all — so the
area estimate spans an order of magnitude. More fixes per day would not help;
only a much longer track could. For a nomadic species, the honest answer may be
that a home range is the wrong summary.
:::

## Task 4 — Ground truth

In Session 5 we built a central-place walker. Because we wrote its rule, we can
compute its **true** 95% home range by simulating it for a very long time.

```{r}
#| cache: true
source("R/simulators.R")
true95 <- truth_area(0.95)
true95
```

Now pretend it is a collared animal: sample it every hour for ~69 days and
estimate its range.

```{r}
#| cache: true
sim <- truth_animal()                           # 5,000 steps of 20 minutes
obs <- sim[seq(1, nrow(sim), by = 3), ]         # an hourly GPS fix
obs$t <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (obs$step - 1) * 20 * 60

sim_pts <- SpatialPoints(obs[, c("x", "y")])
est <- c(
  MCP      = mcp.area(sim_pts, percent = 95, unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]],
  KDE_href = kernel.area(kernelUD(sim_pts, h = "href", grid = 200), percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]],
  KDE_LSCV = kernel.area(suppressWarnings(kernelUD(sim_pts, h = "LSCV", grid = 200)),
                         percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
)

# AKDE: park the simulated animal in UTM 36S so ctmm gets longitude/latitude
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_as_sf(data.frame(x = obs$x + 4e5, y = obs$y + 7.3e6), coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32736),
  4326))
sim_tel <- as.telemetry(data.frame(timestamp = obs$t, location.long = ll[, 1],
                                   location.lat = ll[, 2], individual.local.identifier = "truth"),
                        timeformat = "auto")
sim_fit <- ctmm.select(sim_tel, ctmm.guess(sim_tel, interactive = FALSE))
sim_ci  <- summary(akde(sim_tel, sim_fit), units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6

round(c(est, AKDE = sim_ci[2], AKDE_low = sim_ci[1], AKDE_high = sim_ci[3],
        TRUTH = true95))
```

One animal is one draw: an estimator can be lucky. The fair test repeats the
experiment on many independent animals. That takes ~20 minutes, so it has been
run for you by `R/hr_ground_truth.R`; the results are in
`data/hr_ground_truth.csv`.

```{r}
reps <- read.csv("data/hr_ground_truth.csv")
nrow(reps)
```

### Your turn

**4a.** For each estimator, plot estimate / truth across the replicates.
**4b.** How often does AKDE's 95% confidence interval contain the truth?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center
long <- reps |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(MCP, KDE_href, KDE_LSCV, BBMM, AKDE),
                      names_to = "estimator", values_to = "km2") |>
  mutate(ratio = km2 / true95,
         estimator = factor(estimator, c("MCP", "KDE_href", "KDE_LSCV", "BBMM", "AKDE")))

ggplot(long, aes(estimator, ratio)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#1f6f78", alpha = 0.25, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, size = 1.6, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate / true area",
       title = "Twenty simulated animals, 69 days of hourly fixes each") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
long |>
  group_by(estimator) |>
  summarise(median_ratio = round(median(ratio), 2),
            spread_IQR   = round(IQR(ratio), 2), .groups = "drop")

c(AKDE_CI_covers_truth = mean(reps$AKDE_low <= reps$true95 & reps$AKDE_high >= reps$true95))
```

Every estimator fails in a characteristic way, and now you can see which way:

- **MCP** and **LSCV** sit below the line — too small, for the reasons in the
  slides (convexity cuts both ways; LSCV fragments the UD).
- **The Brownian bridge** is far below the line — not because it is wrong, but
  because it answers a different question: where the animal *went* in 69
  days, not where it *lives*.
- **KDE with $h_\text{ref}$** can land close to the truth for this animal —
  its over-smoothing happens to offset the autocorrelation bias. That is luck
  of the geometry, not a property you can rely on: compare its performance on
  Cilla, whose range is far from a single bivariate normal.
- **AKDE** is the only estimator whose uncertainty is stated, and its
  confidence interval should contain the truth in most replicates.

Estimators are not "right" or "wrong" in general. They are right or wrong
*for a question*, and simulation with a known truth is how you find out which.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You double the fix rate of your collars from hourly to every 30 minutes, for
the same 3 months. What happens to AKDE's confidence interval on the home-range
area?

- [ ] It halves
- [ ] It narrows by a factor of √2
- [x] It barely changes, because the effective sample size depends on how many times the animal crossed its range
- [ ] It widens

::: {.quiz-feedback}
AKDE's effective sample size is roughly the tracking duration divided by the
range-crossing time. Sampling faster adds fixes, but not range crossings. To
narrow the interval you must track for **longer**, not more often.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Which estimator would you use to map the corridors an animal actually used
during a 2-week dispersal event?

- [ ] AKDE
- [x] A Brownian bridge
- [ ] MCP
- [ ] KDE with LSCV

::: {.quiz-feedback}
A dispersal event is non-stationary by definition, so a *range* distribution
is meaningless; you want the **occurrence** distribution — where the animal
went — which is exactly what the Brownian bridge estimates.
:::
:::
